title: A technological capability scale for civilizations from the Kardashev and Barrow scales
abstract: We introduce a technological capability scale that ranks civilizations by the control operations they can perform per second. A control operation is defined as setting one binary degree of freedom of matter to a specified value, whatever its previous state. Building on constructor theory, we sort them into construction and its special cases on information media, namely processing, storage and transfer. The index $Ξ= K + B$ adds to the Kardashev index $K$ an efficiency index $B$ of energy per operation, measured from the thermal floor at the microwave background temperature. The Kardashev scale gives the ceiling for resets of thermally random bits with heat radiated into the present sky, and the Barrow scale gives the floor, which for such a reset is the thermal floor at the heat-rejection temperature at every level. Since 1950 the energy per logic operation has fallen 11.7 orders of magnitude, around 5 through miniaturization. Humanity, at $K = 0.73$, computes with CMOS logic gates at $B = -0.78$ in primary energy. We describe the ultimate technology, at $Ξ= 7.58$, which would dissipate the conjectured largest power $c^5/4G$ into an uncharged, non-rotating black hole near its largest mass in de Sitter space.
summary: This paper introduces a novel technological capability scale, $\Xi$, that merges the Kardashev and Barrow scales to rank civilizations based on their total operational capacity. It quantifies this capacity using the power available and the minimum energy required for fundamental information control operations. The resulting index provides a theoretical framework for understanding the ultimate physical limits of advanced technological societies.
main_problem: To develop a comprehensive technological capability scale for advanced civilizations by synthesizing the Kardashev (energy usage) and Barrow (physical scale) metrics.
main_result: The authors propose a new index, $\Xi = K + B$, which quantifies a civilization's total operational capability by combining its maximum power output ($K$) and its minimum energy cost per operation ($B$).
method: The scale is built upon defining a 'control operation' (setting a binary degree of freedom) and relating the achievable operations ($\Omega$) to the available power ($P$) and the minimum energy cost ($\epsilon$) via $\Omega \le P/\epsilon$.
model_or_system: The model is a theoretical index $\Xi$ that ranks civilizations based on their ability to manipulate matter and information, extending concepts from established astrophysical and thermodynamic scaling laws.
key_observables: The primary observables are the civilization's power level ($P$), the energy per operation ($\epsilon$), and the resulting capability index ($\Xi$).
important_parameters: Key parameters include the Kardashev index ($K$), the efficiency index ($B$), the CMB temperature ($T_0$), and the ultimate power limit $c^5/4G$.
main_assumptions: The scale assumes that the Barrow scale represents the theoretical minimum energy cost possible at any given level, and it relies on defining a fundamental 'control operation' for all technological processes.
paper_structure: The paper is structured to first define the operation and indices (Section II), assign energy levels to the scale (Section III), place humanity and hypothetical civilizations on the scale (Section IV), and finally treat information storage and transfer mechanisms (Section V).
why_interesting: While not focused on specific quantum hardware, the paper deeply engages with fundamental physical limits (Landauer's principle, thermodynamics) that underpin quantum information theory, providing a macro-scale context for quantum computation's ultimate physical constraints.
